subject: Physics
owned_sme_text: Every physical quantity has a magnitude and a unit. Magnitude alone is meaningless until paired with the unit it is measured against. SI is the internationally accepted system of units; the seven base quantities are length (m), mass (kg), time (s), electric current (A), temperature (K), amount of substance (mol), and luminous intensity (cd). All other quantities are derived. For example, velocity has dimension [LT^-1] because it equals displacement divided by time; force has dimension [MLT^-2] because it equals mass times acceleration; energy has dimension [ML^2T^-2]; pressure has dimension [ML^-1T^-2]. Dimensional analysis is a powerful diagnostic tool — it can check whether an equation is dimensionally consistent, it can derive the form of a physical relation up to a dimensionless constant, and it can detect equations that are physically impossible. But dimensional analysis cannot determine pure numerical constants like 2 or pi, it cannot prove a formula correct (only consistent), and it fails for relations that involve transcendental functions like trig or exponentials where the argument must be dimensionless. Significant figures convey the precision of a measurement. The rules for counting are: all non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant; leading zeros are not significant; trailing zeros in a number with a decimal point are significant; trailing zeros without a decimal point are ambiguous. When adding or subtracting, the result has the same number of decimal places as the least precise measurement. When multiplying or dividing, the result has the same number of significant figures as the least precise factor. Accuracy refers to how close a measurement is to the true value; precision refers to how close repeated measurements are to each other. A measurement can be precise but not accurate (consistent but biased), accurate but not precise (close on average but scattered), both, or neither. Errors fall into three classes: systematic errors (consistent bias, usually instrumental or methodological — fixable by calibration), random errors (statistical scatter, reducible by repeated measurement and averaging), and gross errors (mistakes — discardable). The least count of an instrument is the smallest value it can resolve; for a vernier caliper this is usually 0.01 cm and for a screw gauge 0.001 cm. Students often confuse the zero error of an instrument with the least count — zero error is a systematic offset that adds to every reading, while least count is the resolution limit. Common JEE-NEET pitfall: writing the answer with more significant figures than the inputs justify, or forgetting to convert all quantities to SI before substituting into a formula.
